AI disclosure: This article and sample code were prepared with AI assistance. The health values are synthetic demonstration state.

A healing glow has one job: make a real health increase noticeable. It should not decide whether healing occurred, animate a value the game never accepted, or leave an invisible runtime ticking after the health panel closes.

The local recipe keeps those responsibilities separate. A synthetic health change updates a fixed-width bar and its numeric label. A short particle burst then appears around the bar. The particles are feedback; the health value remains authoritative state owned by the host.

## Define the trigger before the appearance

In a game, call the visual trigger after the authoritative state confirms an increase. Do not trigger it simply because the player pressed a heal button. A rejected action, a full-health character, or a delayed server response may make that button press different from a successful heal.

The demonstration starts at 40 out of 100 health. Replay adds 20 points until the synthetic value reaches 100; the next replay returns to 40 so the example can be exercised again. That reset is a demonstration control, not production healing logic. Replace it with the actual state event when integrating the recipe.

For teams choosing a **web game particle editor**, [NixieFX's PixiJS guide](https://nixiefx.com/pixijs-particle-effects/) explains the surrounding export pipeline. The work here is to make the trigger, positioning, and lifetime explicit in a health-bar host.

## Use a small exported effect

The supplied `healing-glow` source has a single non-looping emitter. It schedules 14 particles at the beginning of a short emission window, uses a 0.55-second particle lifetime, and caps the emitter at 20 particles. Those are authored inputs for this recipe, not a universal mobile budget.

The emitter uses a shallow rectangular spawn region to distribute particles around the bar. Its procedural particles need no external texture files or custom material provider. The bar itself is a host UI element; changing the effect must not change its geometry or the calculation of filled health.

Validate and export after editing the source. Keep the compiled bundle beside the application's static assets, then load it through the official export loader. Do not make a generated output file your new authoring source.

## Position feedback using the bar's coordinate system

The runnable fixture uses an untransformed stage and a separate VFX layer. It explicitly selects a downward-Y projection with one pixel per world unit, matching the HUD coordinates. It converts the content's center into stage coordinates before creating a burst. In a transformed HUD, convert that point to the actual effect layer's local coordinate system as well.

The following is the lifecycle shape used by the fixture. It assumes the application, renderer, and exported effect have already been initialized by the supplied loader.

```js
const live = new Set();

function showHealingGlow(stagePoint) {
  // Replace feedback rather than accumulate rapid duplicate bursts.
  for (const old of live) vfx.removeEffect(old, true);
  live.clear();
  live.add(vfx.createEffect(effect, {
    position: [stagePoint.x, stagePoint.y, 0],
    seed: 42
  }));
}

function tick(ticker) {
  vfx.update(ticker.deltaMS / 1000);
  for (const instance of live) {
    if (!instance.isActive) {
      vfx.removeEffect(instance, true);
      live.delete(instance);
    }
  }
}

app.ticker.add(tick);

function closeHealthPanel() {
  app.ticker.remove(tick);
  vfx.destroy();
  live.clear();
}
```

The fixture clamps unusually large frame deltas and gates updates while hidden or paused. The simplified snippet highlights ownership: the host owns the callback, the renderer owns its effect instances, and cleanup removes both responsibilities.

## Decide what happens when healing repeats

Repeated healing can restart a single visual cue, create one cue per event, or accumulate into a stronger presentation. The demo chooses replacement. That choice keeps the example bounded and avoids obscuring the health text after rapid inputs.

The choice is visual, not a data shortcut. If three legitimate heals arrive, all three state changes still need to be processed. Replacing their feedback must not discard their game events. A production host should also avoid treating an older event as new healing after a panel is reopened.

## Exercise cleanup as a visible control

The draft package includes a Dispose button that removes the ticker callback and destroys the VFX renderer. After disposal, replay and pause controls are disabled. Reload to initialize a fresh fixture. This makes the ownership boundary observable instead of leaving it as an unused helper.

Check a normal heal, repeated heals, an inactive panel, and a complete scene teardown. Confirm that finished instances are removed and that no frame callback continues to update a destroyed renderer. Any texture cache introduced later must have its own release policy.

## Keep the recipe's limits explicit

This is a PixiJS screen-space effect. It does not prove equivalent Three.js behavior, GPU depth, lighting, or support for arbitrary authored materials. The supplied export validates without warnings or blockers; future source changes require a new support check.

Try the [runnable healing-bar fixture](/demos/day-07/?mode=heal) and inspect the [complete application source and effect project](/demos/day-07/day-07-source.zip). The fixture includes replay, pause, disposal, and visible diagnostics. Device performance and artist review remain separate checks.
